title: Running Is Not Ready
subtitle: Module 07 — the kubelet's loop, the four boundaries, and what a Pod's status is really telling you

meta.note: Timing comes from the synthesised audio. estSeconds is a planning estimate only. Content authority: assets/content.js unit u7.

beats.title: You are here
beats.narration: Segment six of the spine: the kubelet. A name was written into the API, and nothing has happened on the node yet. This module is what the kubelet does with that name. The four contracts it speaks across, and why a Pod can be Running and still be useless.

visual.spec: REUSE spineLocator with segment six lit.

beats.title: A loop, not an inbox
beats.narration: Nobody tells the kubelet to start a Pod. There is no command, no dispatch, no push. It watches the API for Pods assigned to its node and drives them toward the state those objects describe. Same loop shape as every controller in module three, running on the node instead of the control plane. It coordinates the runtime, the network, storage, secrets, probes, and the status it reports back.

visual.spec: NEW. The kubelet drawn as a reconcile loop anchored to one node, watching the API rather than receiving from it. Draw the push model first and strike it through — no arrow from the scheduler into the kubelet. Then the pull: a watch line up to the API, and six spokes out to the things it coordinates (runtime, network, storage, secrets, probes, status). The six spokes must be legible labels, not icons.

beats.title: The order on the node
beats.narration: Once a Pod is bound, the order on the node is fixed. The sandbox is created first. Its network is attached. Volumes are mounted. Init containers run to completion, in order. Then the application containers start. That order is not arbitrary. The sandbox exists first because it anchors the shared namespaces. A network attachment has to belong to something before a container can join it.

visual.spec: NEW. Five ordered steps filling the stage width: sandbox created, network attached, volumes mounted, init containers (run to completion, in order), app containers start. Each lights in turn and stays lit. Under the first two, a short note on why they come first — the sandbox anchors the namespaces, the attachment needs something to attach to. Lay the steps as a row that wraps, never a fixed-width strip.

beats.title: What the sandbox is for
beats.narration: So the sandbox is the thing that holds a Pod together. Shared network, IPC and UTS namespaces live there, which is what lets containers in one Pod reach each other on localhost. It also means networking is configured before any application container exists. A Pod can therefore have a perfectly healthy runtime and no network at all — the sandbox came up, the attachment did not.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's Sandbox, which already draws the pod sandbox and its shared namespaces. Extend it: show two containers in the Pod reaching each other over localhost through the shared netns, then show the failure case — sandbox present and healthy, attachment absent, containers running with no route out. Keep the namespace labels at the same type scale as the rest; they are the point of the beat.

beats.title: Four contracts, not one runtime
beats.narration: Four acronyms get collapsed into the word runtime, and they are four separate contracts. CRI is the gRPC contract between the kubelet and a runtime like containerd. OCI specifies the lower-level image and runtime primitives underneath that. CNI attaches Pod networking. CSI handles storage. Each has its own failure mode and its own logs, so knowing which boundary broke tells you which log to open.

visual.spec: NEW. Four labelled contracts drawn as boundaries between named parties, not as a flat list: CRI between kubelet and containerd; OCI below containerd, at runc; CNI at the sandbox's network; CSI at the volume. Beside each, its characteristic failure and the log you would read. Fill the stage — this is the beat people screenshot.

beats.title: The kubelet never calls runc
beats.narration: The kubelet speaks CRI and only CRI — a runtime service and an image service, both gRPC. It never calls runc. containerd receives the CRI call and, below that boundary, invokes a runtime that creates the namespaces and cgroups. That lower layer is OCI. The kubelet does not use it directly, and that distinction is usually what an interviewer is probing.

visual.spec: NEW. A vertical stack with one emphasised horizontal line: kubelet — [CRI: runtime service + image service, gRPC] — containerd — [OCI] — runc — namespaces and cgroups. Animate a call descending and stopping at the CRI line to show where the kubelet's reach ends. Draw the kubelet-to-runc arrow people imagine, then strike it through.

beats.title: Phase is not health
beats.narration: Running is a phase. It means the process is alive. Ready is a separate signal, and it means the application will accept traffic. They are set by different mechanisms and they answer different questions. A container can run for hours, be entirely alive, and never be ready — and the Pod's phase will keep saying Running the whole time.

visual.spec: NEW. One Pod, two independent indicators side by side and clearly not linked: phase (Running) and ready (false). Run a clock forward so phase holds steady at Running while ready stays false. Two separate mechanisms feeding them, drawn as separate inputs. The whole beat fails if the two read as one status.

beats.title: Three probes, three jobs
beats.narration: Three probes, three jobs. Startup gates the other two while a slow application initialises, and nothing else runs until it passes. Liveness restarts the container when it fails. Readiness removes the Pod from endpoints without restarting anything. Choosing the wrong one is the classic mistake. A liveness probe pointed at a slow dependency turns that dependency into a restart loop, and the restarts make it worse.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's Probes. Extend it with the consequence column: startup → gates the others, liveness → restarts the container, readiness → leaves endpoints. Then the trap: a liveness probe pointed at a slow dependency, restarting on a timer, with the restart count climbing and the dependency no healthier. Let the loop run long enough to read as a loop.

beats.title: Running, receiving nothing
beats.narration: When a Pod is Running and receives nothing, phase is exactly what misled you. Follow the chain instead. Is the container ready. Is the Pod in the EndpointSlice. Does the Service selector actually match its labels, and does the target port match the container port. Each link is checkable in a second, and the first one that fails is the answer.

visual.spec: NEW. A four-link chain, each link a question with a real check beside it: ready → EndpointSlice membership → selector matches labels → targetPort matches containerPort. Break one link and show traffic stopping there. The Pod's phase sits above the chain reading Running throughout, unchanged, to make the point that it is not part of the chain.

beats.title: Deletion is not a transaction
beats.narration: Deletion is not a transaction. The grace period starts. The PreStop hook runs, then TERM is delivered. At the same time, not before, the Pod is being removed from endpoints. Those two run concurrently, so traffic can still arrive at a container that has already been told to shut down. A PreStop sleep is a real fix for that, not a hack. When the grace period expires, the process is killed.

visual.spec: NEW. Two parallel timelines on one clock, deliberately not synchronised. Top: grace period starts, PreStop runs, TERM delivered, force kill at expiry. Bottom: endpoint removal propagating through EndpointSlice to the data plane. Show the overlap window shaded, with a request landing on the already-terminating container inside it. Then show a PreStop sleep widening the gap so the overlap closes.

beats.title: The API repeats what it was told
beats.narration: Pod status is reported by the kubelet, asynchronously. If the node loses connectivity the kubelet stops reporting, and the last value simply persists. The API will show Running for a Pod on a node that is already gone. The node lease has to expire, the node controller has to mark the node unreachable, and only then do other controllers react.

visual.spec: NEW. A node reporting status up to the API on a tick. Cut the link: the tick stops, and the API's stored value freezes at Running while the node visibly goes dark. Show the lease counting down, the node controller marking unreachable, and only then downstream controllers moving. Put the elapsed time on screen so the delay is readable as a duration, not an instant.

beats.title: Back to the spine
beats.narration: Segment six, then. A failure here has a signature: the Pod has a node, the node accepted it, and something on that node did not finish. The API tells you very little, because the API is only repeating what the kubelet last said. The next segment is the one the sandbox was waiting for — the network attachment itself. That is module eight.

visual.spec: REUSE, reversed: segment six shrinks back into the spine, segment seven lights to preview the next module.
